USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture and pursue the 90-day negotiation window with discipline. Do not escalate further until talks have played out, but do not offer premature concessions either. Use the Huawei enforcement action as leverage in parallel while keeping trade and law enforcement formally separate to preserve negotiating credibility.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is mildly favorable to the US (-0.25) because the US holds meaningful leverage: $250B in tariffs are already in force, the Huawei/Meng arrest signals willingness to use non-tariff tools against China's tech champions, and China's economy is under pressure from the tariff regime. However, the threat is NOT deeply negative because: (1) the trade deficit with China has actually widened to a record $43.1B in October (USCC Dec bulletin), undermining the core tariff rationale; (2) US markets are in sharp correction — S&P 500 down ~7.8% in December alone, worst December since 1931 (CNN, Dec 18), and down 4.8% YTD (NYT, Dec 17); (3) 10-year Treasury yields have fallen from 3.23% in October to 2.77% by Dec 19, signaling growth fears; (4) trade subtracted 1.78% from Q3 GDP (MBT Magazine, Nov 30); (5) soybean exports to China collapsed from 57% of US exports to under 2% (MBT Magazine); (6) the G20 truce is fragile — Chinese state media won't confirm the 90-day frame, and the Meng arrest (Dec 1) plus China's detention of two Canadians (Dec 10) has injected massive uncertainty. The action score (-0.15, negotiate) reflects the correct posture: the 90-day window is the appropriate channel, the domestic economic costs of further escalation are mounting (farm belt pain, rising SME bankruptcies, retail price increases coming in spring 2019), and the market is signaling it wants resolution not escalation. But there is no reason to concede — the US has tariff leverage already applied and the Huawei card as a pressure point. The risk of escalation is that China retaliates further and the market sell-off deepens into a broader economic downturn; the risk of concession is that it undermines the entire Section 301 strategy without extracting structural reforms on IP, forced tech transfer, or Made in China 2025.
key_factors: US-China trade deficit hit record $43.1B in October despite tariffs
S&P 500 worst December since 1931, down ~7.8% month-to-date
10Y Treasury yield fell from 3.23% (Oct) to 2.77% (Dec 19) — growth fears
G20 truce fragile: conflicting US/China readouts, 90-day clock ticking
Huawei CFO arrest (Dec 1) adds non-tariff leverage but complicates talks
China detained two Canadians (Dec 10) in apparent retaliation
US soybean exports to China collapsed to <2% of total
SME bankruptcies rising, retail price increases expected spring 2019
Fed widely expected to raise rates 4th time in 2018, adding to market pressure

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest)
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5-10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.

In October 2018, the U.S. goods trade deficit increased 22.3 percent year-on-year to reach a record high of $43.1 billion; declines in export categories targeted by retaliatory tariffs contributed to the sharp deficit increase
The Dow and S&P 500 were each down about 7.8% through Monday. That's the largest drop for each key market barometer since 1931

Trade served as a fairly significant drag to GDP, subtracting 1.78 percent from third quarter results. Soybean exports to China accounted for less than 2 percent of total U.S. soybean exports in August 2018.
The arrest of Meng Wanzhou, scion of a Chinese telecommunications giant, came the same day as Trump's self-described extraordinary meeting with Xi in Argentina
